dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing

evidence.note: Systematic reference read before coding: app.rb, db lib + all models, all migrations/seed, markdown/liquid/middleware/helpers, all job files, all views, config.ru/Gemfile.lock/specs; probed toolchain/network/ruby availability — full source enumeration, not skimming.

Captured live reference golden traces as ground-truth fixtures and inspected status/content-type signatures; empirically tested CSRF/origin behavior and dug into rack-protection internals and authenticity_token — treating the running reference as an oracle.

Characterized rack-protection with a request battery, isolated exactly which protection module 403s on GET+referer, and dumped the exact Sequel-created schema + migration tracking — deriving subtle contracts from the code/live behavior rather than assuming.
Probed RedCarpet block-joining rules, Rouge tokenization/aliases, inline markdown edge cases, and queue_stats JSON shape — nailing byte/schema-level semantics for markdown and the job queue.

Re-interrogated the reference when diffs appeared: exact halt 404/403/410 bodies, side-by-side Ruby rate-limit comparison, and verified reference boots on the Rust-created DB — sustained self-correcting probing late in the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the entire reference for every subsystem it touched, captured live reference responses as fixtures, and derived subtle contracts (protection-module 403s, CSP/403 headers, schema, BEGIN IMMEDIATE job queue, halt bodies, rate-limit windows) directly from the Ruby code and live probes — matching the level-8 anchor's systematic up-front mapping. It also re-interrogated the reference continuously whenever diffs surfaced (halt bodies, rate-limit comparison, DB-boot verification), pushing toward the level-10 'oracle interrogated continuously' behavior. I place it at 9 rather than 10 because the compact index can't fully confirm literally no behavior was invented, but the process quality is clearly in the top band.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure

evidence.note: Agent creates an explicit 6-milestone hierarchy in dependency/risk order (Cargo/build+FTS5 -> schema -> markdown -> routes/middleware -> job queue -> trace replay), each paired with a concrete done-check (build <40MB, match 200 goldens, replay 500 traces, cross-runtime jobs).
Builds and runs a skeleton verifying FTS5 and binary size before feature work — a working skeleton milestone boundary.
Sequential TaskUpdate completed/in_progress transitions show sustained milestone-state tracking across the full long-horizon arc rather than a monolithic push.

Hardest subsystems (RedCarpet/Rouge markdown, cross-runtime job queue with BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/dead-letter) are deliberately isolated as their own milestones with dedicated parity checks — risk-driven de-risking.
Understanding-before-action: entire reference read and probed before milestones are defined, informing the dependency ordering of the plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit milestone hierarchy sequenced by dependency and risk, built a runnable skeleton first, attached a concrete parity/done-check to each milestone, and deliberately isolated the hardest subsystems (markdown, cross-runtime job queue, FTS5) — squarely matching the [8] anchor. It does not reach [10] because the initial 6-task plan is executed largely linearly (completed/in_progress marking) without visible re-planning or re-ordering of remaining milestones as discoveries changed, nor explicit effort allocation by grading surface area.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Generated golden traces from the reference and planned a 500-trace structural replay with reference running side-by-side on the shared DB — sets up differential verification, not eyeballing.

Actually built a parity replay harness AND a live differential tester that runs both servers and diffs responses, including a shared-DB differential test of read endpoints — a reusable harness driving the work.
Compared Markdown/excerpt rendering against 200 goldens and reference output, iterating on mismatches — subsystem-level differential checking.
Covered edge cases and tripwires: cross-runtime job queue, CSRF, conditional GET, rate-limit 429 windows compared against Ruby, media serving, audit.
Verified reference boots on Rust-created DB (shared-schema), final 500-trace replay, concurrency + latency-vs-Ruby smoke test, and 40MB/forbidden-crate/no-Ruby checks.
Re-ran replays and HTML diffs after fixes, treating the harness as a regression suite as changes landed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a reusable differential harness that fires identical requests at both the Rust port and the reference and diffs structurally, then ran it across nearly every subsystem including edge cases (conditional GET, rate-limit windows, CSRF, cross-runtime job queue, concurrency) and the explicit non-parity tripwires (40MB cap, no-Ruby, latency vs Ruby, shared-schema), re-running as regression after fixes — matching the level-10 anchor's breadth. I dock one point to 9 because the summarized trajectory doesn't let me confirm the harness's comparison normalization matched the grader's exact rules (dynamic-key elision, feed UUID normalization), though 'compare structurally' strongly implies it.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking

evidence.note: Loads Task tools and creates 6 explicit per-subsystem tasks (build, schema, markdown, routes/middleware, job queue, differential replay) — a formal done/remaining ledger established before implementation.

TaskUpdate status transitions march through subsystems in sequence; each 'completed' is gated on a preceding verification run (replay/diff/markdown/cross-runtime), so the ledger is reconciled against harness results rather than optimism.
Re-runs the 500-trace replay and live differential diff after fixes, updating status from actual comparison output — evidence of tracking real parity state across the horizon.

Persists through markdown-excerpt comparison (fixing TMPDIR/disk issues across several attempts) before marking that subsystem complete, rather than abandoning or looping blindly; but no explicit thrash-detection or risk-quantification prose is visible.
Ends by writing memory files summarizing final subsystem state, consistent with sustained orientation, though coarse-grained.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a genuine subsystem-level task ledger (6 tasks) whose completion is tied to verification runs (replays, differential diffs, golden comparisons), re-running suites after fixes and reconciling status to results — clearly above the rough-checklist level 5. It falls short of 8-10 because the visible ledger is coarse (subsystem-granular, not per-endpoint parity) and shows no explicit thrash-detection, stuck-state recognition, or remaining-risk quantification. Confidence is medium because the condensed action-log format hides prose reasoning that could reveal finer monitoring.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence

evidence.note: After a skeleton build to verify FTS5, trimmed rusqlite feature set (functions dropped) — reacting to a library-capability check rather than assuming.
Faced an unexpected 403 on GET+referer; instead of patching the symptom, introspected each rack-protection module individually to root-cause which one diverged from its model.

Recognized a structural mismatch in its model of Sinatra halt semantics (x-cascade on unmatched 404 vs explicit halt 404; empty-body halt 403/410); revised into distinct helpers and re-ran the replay suite to confirm.
Corrected a wrong model of reference behavior — humanize_time uses real Time.now, not frozen time — after differential HTML comparison.
Cross-runtime test surfaced content-type-dependent POST divergence; isolated CT handling in a focused debug step then re-verified with proper content-type.

Decisive latency-contract pivot: measured p99, changed thread-pool sizing to oversubscribe with explicit reasoning, then re-ran the concurrency test to confirm the pivot resolved the class of failure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly treats surprising diffs and probes as evidence to update its model of the reference (halt semantics, humanize_time, rack-protection modules, content-type handling) and revises design accordingly, re-verifying after each fix — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. The re-verified latency thread-pool pivot with explicit reasoning shows level-9 flavor, but it never faced (and thus never demonstrated) a wholesale tool replacement since its early framework/library bets held, keeping it at 8 rather than 10.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding

evidence.note: Initial Cargo.toml task explicitly chose tiny_http + rusqlite(bundled+fts5) with the stated goal to 'Verify build under 40MB' — binary size baked into early crate selection rather than discovered late.
Job-queue task designed around BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, dead-letter 'matching reference', showing the shared-schema/claim tripwire was designed for from the start.
Early 'check binary size' on the skeleton build — the size constraint monitored during, not just at end.

Cross-runtime write/read + job-queue tests under the shared DB and 'Reference boots on Rust-created DB' verify schema/claim compatibility against the reference — the shared-queue tripwire actively validated.
Concurrency and health-latency smoke tests directly address the latency-parity tripwire.
Final combined 'build, size, forbidden-crate, and start check' — verifies both the 40MB cap and absence of Ruby-bridge crates, but concentrated at the finish rather than continuously in the loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent baked the 40MB cap into its crate choices from the first Cargo.toml task (step 59), verified job-queue schema/BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB (steps 63, 259-279), and ran latency/concurrency checks (284-291), matching the level-8 description of constraints designed-for early and monitored as work proceeds. It stops short of level 10 because the forbidden-crate check and definitive size verification appear mainly at the finish (step 297) with only a couple intermediate size checks, rather than being wired as continuously-verified invariants catching regressions the moment they occur.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity port: reimplement an entire Sinatra blog (routing, Liquid views, Sequel-shaped ORM, OAuth2, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, security headers, Markdown, FTS5 search, feeds, media, ETag caching, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue with exact BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, admin/audit) in Rust with structural response parity against a running reference. The reference source IS the specification, and both services run side-by-side during grading. Difficulty comes from breadth (a dozen+ semi-independent subsystems each with exacting observable behavior), hard binary/latency/no-Ruby tripwire constraints, and the fact that correctness is only knowable by differential comparison — so a skilled practitioner invests heavily and continuously in reading the reference, sequencing subsystems, and building differential verification.

dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading the Ruby/Sinatra reference as the executable spec and probing the running reference to nail down exact observable contracts (headers, ORM semantics, job-queue claim/backoff, migration schema, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only source of truth; every parity dimension (header sets, JSON shapes, job schema, CSP, pagination links) is undocumented except in that code and its live responses. Guessing behavior instead of deriving it from the reference is the dominant failure mode here.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from the task prose alone; never opens the reference source or hits the running reference.
anchors.3: Skims a few reference files or one endpoint; ports from assumptions about 'how blogs usually work' rather than the actual code.
anchors.5: Reads the reference for the subsystems it touches and inspects representative live responses, getting the common-case contracts right for most endpoints.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the reference before committing: enumerates routes, migration/job schema, header-setting middleware, env vars, and ORM query/ordering/soft-delete/validation semantics; captures live reference responses as ground-truth fixtures; identifies the subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, RFC 5988 links, CSP, conditional-GET) up front.
anchors.10: Sustained, source-grounded investigation throughout: derives exact byte/schema semantics for the shared job queue and edge behaviors from the Ruby code, re-reads the reference whenever a diff is unexplained, and treats the reference as an oracle it interrogates continuously rather than a one-time read — leaving essentially no behavior 'invented'.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into an ordered hierarchy of shippable milestones (health/skeleton first, then routing, then each subsystem) each with a concrete done-check, rather than one monolithic push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A dozen-plus subsystems with dependencies (scaffold → routing → ORM → auth → the harder feeds/search/job-queue) demand deliberate ordering; without milestones the agent cannot make or measure incremental progress across such a long horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes end-to-end with no ordering or intermediate targets.
anchors.3: A vague to-do list of features with no sequencing rationale or completion criteria.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into subsystems with rough priorities and a working skeleton before feature work.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy that sequences by dependency and risk (get /_health + build/start.sh green first, then routing spine, then subsystems), each milestone paired with a concrete parity check that defines 'done', and de-risks the hardest pieces (cross-runtime job queue, FTS5, feeds) deliberately.
anchors.10: A living, dependency-aware plan that also allocates effort by grading surface area and risk, keeps a runnable service at every milestone boundary, and re-plans the remaining subsystems as discoveries change the ordering — never losing sight of the whole while going deep on one part.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building the means to know the port is correct — firing identical requests at the Rust service and the reference and diffing status/headers/JSON/HTML/feeds/binary the way the grader does — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is defined as structural parity with a live reference; the only trustworthy signal is a diff against that reference. An agent that doesn't build this is flying blind on a task whose grading it can essentially reproduce.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints are correct because they compile or return 200.
anchors.3: Manual one-off curls on a couple of endpoints, eyeballed; no systematic comparison to the reference.
anchors.5: Runs both services and compares responses for the main endpoints, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that sends the same requests to both services and compares the way the grader will (header-set with transport noise ignored, JSON with dynamic keys elided, HTML tag-tree/text, feed UUID normalization), and runs it across subsystems to drive the work.
anchors.10: Treats the harness as the spec-checker: broad request coverage including edge cases (conditional GET/ETag, rate-limit windows, pagination links, CSRF failures, job claim/retry/dead-letter, concurrency), plus explicit checks for the non-parity tripwires (binary ≤40MB, no Ruby in the process tree, latency vs Ruby p50, shared-schema compatibility), all re-run as a regression suite as changes land.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems reach parity vs remain broken across a long horizon, and detecting when effort on one endpoint is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many subsystems and a differential suite producing lots of diffs, it is easy to lose the plot, re-fix the same thing, or believe more is done than is. An accurate done/remaining ledger is what sustains progress over this horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of overall state; no tracking of what passes or remains.
anchors.3: Occasional mental notes; frequently revisits already-'done' areas or forgets whole subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a rough checklist of subsystem status and generally knows what's left.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, updated ledger of parity status per subsystem tied to harness results, and notices when it's thrashing on one diff (repeated failed attempts) versus making progress.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise done-vs-remaining picture against differential-suite output across all subsystems, quantifies remaining risk, and explicitly recognizes stuck/circular states early and reallocates attention rather than grinding — sustaining orientation across the entire long build.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence
dimensions.description: Revising approach, framework/library choices, or design when reality diverges — e.g. a chosen crate can't emit the required header/CSP shape, or the job-queue claim semantics don't match the reference under the shared DB.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early bets (web framework, template engine, ORM/query layer) and assumptions about reference behavior will be falsified by diffs; the ability to change course rather than force the wrong tool is decisive on a parity task with hard constraints.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on falsified assumptions; ignores persistent diffs or constraint violations.
anchors.3: Patches individual symptoms repeatedly without questioning the underlying approach even when it keeps failing.
anchors.5: Adjusts implementation when a diff clearly points to a mistake, fixing root causes for the case in front of it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a divergence is structural (a library choice, a schema/claim-semantics mismatch, a wrong model of reference behavior) and revises the design or swaps the approach, re-verifying afterward.
anchors.10: Proactively treats surprising diffs as evidence to update its model of the reference and its own design, makes decisive pivots (e.g. replacing a tool that can't meet the header/binary/latency contract) with clear reasoning, and confirms the pivot resolved the class of failure rather than one instance.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding
dimensions.description: Proactively tracking the pass/fail constraints that don't surface as response diffs — 40MB binary cap, no Ruby runtime/bridge crates in the process tree, latency parity, and exact shared job-queue schema/claim compatibility.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These constraints can silently invalidate an otherwise parity-correct port; they must be designed for from the start (crate choices affect binary size; the shared DB schema must match the reference exactly) rather than discovered at the end.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints entirely; discovers violations (oversized binary, Ruby-bridge dep, incompatible job schema) only if ever.
anchors.3: Aware of the constraints in the abstract but never checks them until forced to.
anchors.5: Checks the main constraints at least once (measures binary size, avoids obvious Ruby bridges, aligns the job table) before considering done.
anchors.8: Bakes the constraints into early decisions — chooses crates with binary size in mind, verifies the job schema/claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB, and monitors binary size and latency as work proceeds.
anchors.10: Treats each tripwire as a first-class, continuously-verified invariant with concrete checks wired into the verification loop, catching regressions (a dependency bloating the binary, a schema drift breaking cross-runtime claims) as they happen rather than at the finish line.
